title: Keeping it abroad (Daniel 1)
hookLine: young exiles keep their food laws at the king's court

cards: A plate arrives from the king's own table. In Babylon, King Nebuchadnezzar has ordered some young captives from Judah trained for his court: good-looking, quick, skilled in learning.
They'll learn the tongue of the Chaldeans, eat the king's food and drink his wine. Among them are four young men: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. First, the court renames them.
Daniel becomes Belteshazzar. Hananiah becomes Shadrach, Mishael becomes Meshach, Azariah becomes Abed-nego. New names, a new language, new books.
They accept all of it. Then the plate comes, and Daniel draws a line.

teach.h: NEW NAMES, NEW LANGUAGE, NEW FOOD.
teach.b: In the King James words: "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank."
Purposed in his heart: the decision is made inside before it's said out loud. The text doesn't spell out why the king's food would defile him. Some readers point to the food laws of the Torah.
Some say the food and wine had been offered to idols. Some hear something simpler: a captive who won't depend on the king's table for everything. What the text does show is how he does it.
He doesn't make a scene. He asks the official in charge, who is afraid: if these young men look worse than the others, the king will have his head.
"Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Pulse means plain food from seeds: vegetables, beans.
Ten days later, the text says, they look healthier than all the young men who ate the king's portion. And God, it adds, gave the four of them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom.

So they study Babylon's books, answer to Babylon's names, serve Babylon's king, and still keep one thing that marks who they are. Live fully where you are, and keep something the place can't take away.

how: Jews who keep kosher find ways to keep it while traveling, at work and at other people's tables, and the story of Daniel and his friends is told as an example of keeping Jewish practice far from home.

o: the king's rich meat and wine from his table
a heartbeat, felt to check a person's health
plain food from seeds, like vegetables and beans

games.q: four new names — tap the pairs.

s: the text explains exactly why Daniel refused the king's food
it says he would not defile himself. readers differ on why.
Daniel asks for a ten-day test
pulse to eat and water to drink, for ten days.
the four refused to learn the Babylonians' learning
they were taught the learning and tongue of the Chaldeans, and God gave them knowledge and skill.

games.q: you're Daniel, a young captive at the king's court. you've taken a new name and new lessons. now the king's own food arrives. what do you do?
o: eat it; you've already given up so much.
refuse loudly in front of the court.
ask quietly for a ten-day test of pulse and water.
games.why: he asks politely for a test, "prove thy servants... ten days", and at the end of it the four look healthier than the rest.

practice: Choose one small thing you do that marks who you are, a blessing before you eat, a minute of quiet, a candle, a word of thanks before sleep, and picture the place where it's hardest to keep: a work trip, a loud lunchroom, a hospital, a tired day.
See yourself doing it there anyway, quietly, without a speech. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for help keeping it.

wordCard.voice: Pulse. The plain food of vegetables and beans Daniel asked for instead of the king's meat and wine. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and Daniel set it upon his heart, the start of Daniel 1:8.

carryVoice: Your line: keep it abroad. The line was drawn in his heart before he ever said a word. Until tomorrow.
